children: Young defense and space companies are increasingly using special purpose acquisition companies to reach the stock market as enthusiasm for military technology, satellites and drones accelerates, Reuters reported Monday.

Six defense, space or satellite businesses have announced SPAC mergers in 2026, twice the number recorded during all of last year. The transactions represent about 10% of this year’s SPAC deals, according to SPACInsider data cited by Reuters.

For investors, the trend creates more opportunities to back emerging defense technologies but also brings considerable risk. Many of these companies have limited revenue, depend heavily on government contracts and require substantial capital before reaching commercial scale. SPAC transactions can also dilute shareholders and may receive less scrutiny than conventional initial public offerings.

SPACs raise money first and later merge with private businesses seeking public listings. The structure lets companies negotiate valuations and arrange financing before announcing a transaction. That can be attractive to defense contractors facing long product-development schedules and unpredictable government orders.

Propulsion-system maker Ursa Major agreed in August to go public through a SPAC merger valuing the company at about $2.3 billion. The company plans to use the proceeds to expand domestic production of engines for missiles and rockets as customer demand outpaces available manufacturing capacity.

Quantum Space and autonomous-aircraft developer Elroy Air also announced SPAC deals in June. Quantum Space is developing spacecraft for orbital transportation, satellite servicing and refueling. Elroy Air has received a $46 million Army contract to develop an autonomous hybrid-electric aircraft.
More transactions could follow. Nine SPACs are looking for defense or space acquisitions and collectively hold about $2.35 billion in trust, according to SPACInsider.

Traditional IPO activity is rising too. At least seven defense and space companies have completed IPOs this year as businesses seek to benefit from growing demand for satellite networks, communications technology and lower-cost weapons systems.

Government spending provides another tailwind. The Trump administration has proposed increasing the fiscal 2027 national defense budget to roughly $1.5 trillion, compared with $901 billion enacted for 2026. The proposal emphasizes ships, aircraft, missile defense and advanced military technology, though final spending levels require congressional approval.

Modern warfare is also opening the door for newer contractors. The expanded use of drones and autonomous systems in Ukraine and the Middle East has encouraged governments to seek less expensive weapons that can be produced more quickly than many traditional platforms.

Investors should nevertheless expect uneven results. Supply-chain disruptions, contract delays and dependence on a small number of government customers can make revenue volatile. Additional financing may also reduce existing investors’ ownership stakes.

Recent gains by publicly traded space companies have helped restore interest in the SPAC market. Still, the sector’s improved performance does not eliminate the central risk: investors may be asked to value ambitious technology and projected government demand long before either produces dependable profits.

title: Defense, space startups take SPAC route as investor interest soars
